name: 3Blue1Brown (Grant Sanderson)
shortDescription: Mathematics rebuilt visually, so the ideas arrive as pictures with reasons attached rather than as procedures to memorise.
longDescription: Grant Sanderson's stated goal is to use animation to elucidate and motivate topics that are otherwise tricky, and the channel is the clearest demonstration on YouTube of what that means. The recurring form is a question — what a convolution actually is, why the central limit theorem holds, what a Laplace transform does — answered by building the idea up geometrically until the formula becomes obvious rather than given. Sixty-five of the last two hundred uploads run past twenty minutes and fifty-eight sit between three and nineteen. This is not a course and there are no exercises; the value for a self-teacher is that it repairs intuition for topics you may have passed exams in without ever understanding.
notFor: Anyone needing practice problems, exam technique, or coverage of a syllabus. Watching this is not the same as being able to do the mathematics.

categories.why: Rebuilds the intuition underneath a formula, which is exactly what is missing when someone can compute an answer but has no idea what they computed.
categories.evidence: A catalogue built on visual derivations of core mathematical objects — convolution, entropy, the central limit theorem, Laplace transforms — from an author whose stated method is animation-led explanation.

entryVideo.title: But what is a convolution?
entryVideo.whyThisOne: A concept most people first meet as an intimidating integral, made visual and obvious — a fair sample of what the channel does to everything.

caveats: No exercises, no sequence, no syllabus coverage. It repairs understanding; it does not build the ability to solve problems on its own.

name: Abbey Sharp
shortDescription: A registered dietitian whose main subject is why diets fail and what the industry selling them is actually doing.
longDescription: Abbey Sharp is a registered dietitian and the founder of a food media company, and while the channel carries recipes and kitchen content, its substantial work is critical: why restrictive dieting produces the reward cycle that makes it feel effective, why willpower framing keeps failing people, how diet culture has been reconstituted as algorithmic feed conditioning. She also reacts to specific health claims circulating online, including the ones that attribute ordinary symptoms to a fashionable diagnosis. That orientation is what makes her the right creator for a category adjacent to disordered eating: the qualification here is a professional one, and the message is mostly that the thing being sold to you does not work.
notFor: Anyone wanting a weight-loss protocol. The argument runs the other way, and if you want a deficit calculator this will frustrate you.

categories.why: Comes at the subject from why restriction fails rather than how to restrict harder, which is the only responsible starting point in a category this close to disordered eating.
categories.evidence: A registered dietitian publishing sustained analysis of dieting psychology, the reward mechanics of restrictive diets, and the marketing of diet culture, alongside reactions to specific circulating health claims.

entryVideo.title: The Psychology of Dieting: Why Willpower Keeps Failing You
entryVideo.whyThisOne: Reframes repeated failure as a predictable result of the method rather than a personal defect, which is the reframe most people in this category need first.

categories.why: Checks specific viral nutrition claims against professional knowledge, including the ones that pin ordinary symptoms on a fashionable cause.
categories.evidence: A recurring format reacting to circulating health and nutrition claims as a dietitian, including on attributing common symptoms to thyroid dysfunction.

entryVideo.title: Fatigue, Hair Loss, Brain Fog and Weight Gain: Is Your Thyroid Actually to Blame? (Dietitian Reacts)
entryVideo.whyThisOne: A very common set of symptoms and a very common online explanation for them, examined by someone qualified to weigh it.

caveats: Runs a food media business and takes brand work, so read product content accordingly. Much of the channel is recipes rather than the critical material this entry is about. Education, not treatment — disordered eating needs a clinician.

name: Abbie Emmons
shortDescription: A novelist teaching fiction craft through short technique videos and long write-along sessions, wrapped in a substantial paid ecosystem.
longDescription: Abbie Emmons is a published novelist whose channel description frames the work as teaching writers to harness the psychology of storytelling. The teaching is craft-level and specific: subtext, distinguishing two narrators' voices in dual point of view, what makes a character's motivations genuinely complex, how a flashback earns its place. Output is now dominated by short clips, with around a hundred and twenty of the last two hundred uploads running two minutes or less, but roughly fifty long uploads sit behind them and split into two kinds — ten-to-twenty-minute craft lessons, and ninety-to-hundred-minute silent write-along sessions with no instruction in them at all. Nearly every description routes to her book, her paid programme, or a free handout that requires an email address.
notFor: Anyone allergic to a funnel, or wanting craft advice grounded in anything other than one working novelist's own practice.

categories.why: Works at the sentence and scene level with side-by-side rewrites, so you can see the difference between a weak version and a strong one rather than being told there is one.
categories.evidence: The long-form catalogue is craft instruction on named techniques — subtext, dual point-of-view voice, character motivation, flashback construction — several with downloadable handouts and timestamped frameworks.

entryVideo.title: How to Write Subtext (So Readers Can Read Between the Lines)
entryVideo.whyThisOne: Uses paired before-and-after examples throughout, which shows you both the technique and how she teaches in one sitting.

caveats: Sells a book and a paid programme that most videos point to. The very long uploads are mostly silent writing sessions, not lessons — check the length before committing an evening.

name: Addiction Policy Forum
shortDescription: A non-profit interviewing addiction researchers and clinicians — education about dependence with nothing being sold at the end of it.
longDescription: Addiction Policy Forum describes itself as a nationwide non-profit working to eliminate addiction as a major health problem, headquartered in Washington DC. The format is interviews with named academics and clinicians rather than personal testimony or treatment marketing: the mechanisms and models of recovery with a researcher who studies them, measured stigma in the general population, emerging treatment approaches, what a specific use disorder is and who is at risk. Twenty-two of fifty recent uploads run past twenty minutes and twenty-five sit in the mid-length band, with a fourteen-minute median, so this is substantial material rather than clips. It also carries short practical explainers, including on naloxone. The absence of a commercial interest is the point: nobody here profits from your treatment decision.
notFor: Anyone in crisis or needing help now — this is education about a field, not a route into care, and it cannot assess your situation. It is also US-centric in its policy framing.

categories.why: Explains dependence and recovery through the people who research them, with no treatment programme to sell — which is rare enough in this field to be the deciding factor.
categories.evidence: A registered non-profit publishing interviews with named addiction researchers and clinicians on recovery mechanisms, stigma measurement and treatment approaches, alongside practical explainers such as naloxone use.

entryVideo.title: Addiction Recovery: Processes, Mechanisms, and Models with Dr. John Kelly
entryVideo.whyThisOne: A researcher explaining what recovery actually consists of, which is the frame worth having before encountering anyone selling a route through it.

caveats: Education, never assessment or treatment. If you or someone else is in danger, this is not the resource — alcohol and some other withdrawals can be medically serious and need supervision. US policy focus throughout.

name: Alan Becker Tutorials
shortDescription: A closed archive whose main asset is a complete, well-made series on the twelve principles of animation.
longDescription: Alan Becker's tutorial channel is a small companion to his animation work, and it has been dormant since November 2019. Sixty-seven videos, fifty of them between three and nineteen minutes, with a median of eight. Much of it teaches a specific piece of software — Adobe Flash and its successor Animate — which is exactly the kind of material that ages badly, and it has. What has not aged is the series on the twelve principles of animation, published complete in one twenty-four-minute video, which explains squash and stretch, anticipation, timing, arcs and the rest with animated demonstrations of each. Those principles predate the software by decades and outlive it. There are also behind-the-scenes commentaries on his own animations with the working process visible.
notFor: Anyone looking for current tooling. The software tutorials are for a version of an application that has moved on, and nothing new is coming.

categories.why: The twelve principles are the one part of animation that no software change invalidates, and this is a clear, complete, demonstrated version of them.
categories.evidence: A full series on the twelve principles of animation published as a single complete video with animated demonstrations, alongside process commentaries on his own work.

entryVideo.title: 12 Principles of Animation (Official Full Series)
entryVideo.whyThisOne: The whole foundation in twenty-four minutes, and the only thing on this channel that is as useful now as when it was made.

caveats: Dormant since November 2019, and most of the catalogue teaches a superseded version of one application. Treat it as one excellent series plus an archive.

name: Alexander Bromley
shortDescription: Long-form analysis of strength programmes and the history of strength sport — programme design taken apart rather than sold.
longDescription: Bromley's channel runs unusually long for the strength corner of YouTube: of fifty recent uploads, nineteen exceed twenty minutes with an eighteen-minute median, and several pass forty. The useful strand is programme analysis — taking a named training template and working through what it actually does, why its progression is arranged that way, and what claim it is making. A video on a bench programme promising fifty-three pounds in three weeks becomes an explanation of daily undulating periodisation rather than either an endorsement or a dunk. The other strand, and it is large, is the history and biography of strength sport: the greatest deadlifter, the reign of a particular powerlifter, where the squat came from. That is good listening and it is not programme design.
notFor: Anyone wanting a programme to follow tomorrow, or short answers. The channel has no description, no beginner on-ramp, and expects you to already train.

categories.why: Explains why a programme is built the way it is, so you can judge a template against your own situation instead of running it on faith.
categories.evidence: Long-form breakdowns of named strength programmes and periodisation models, alongside a large catalogue on the history and practice of competitive strength sport.

entryVideo.title: the split that claims +53lbs to your Bench Press in 21 days (DUP Explained)
entryVideo.whyThisOne: Takes an extravagant claim and uses it to teach the underlying periodisation model, which is the channel doing what it is best at.

caveats: A large share of the catalogue is strength-sport history rather than training instruction. Sells programming and books, and the channel carries no description at all.

name: Alexander Lyon Communication Coach
shortDescription: A tenured communication professor teaching workplace communication — empathy, listening, teamwork and leadership — in a plain lecture style.
longDescription: Alexander Lyon states on the channel that he is a full-time tenured professor at a public college in New York with more than twenty years of workshops and consulting behind him, and the material reads that way: structured, unhurried, closer to a lecture than to social-media coaching. Roughly half of recent output is short clips, but around eighty videos in the last two hundred run between three and nineteen minutes and a further fourteen exceed twenty, including full mini-classes. The framing is organisational rather than personal, aimed at people who manage others or want to. It fits viewers who prefer a named framework and a slower pace over dense editing and hooks.
notFor: Anyone who finds a lecture format dull, or who wants social and dating applications rather than workplace ones.

categories.why: Teaches listening as a set of teachable moves rather than an attitude, and is willing to spend half an hour on it.
categories.evidence: An academic communication specialist whose longest-form teaching on the channel is a free mini-class on empathic communication.

entryVideo.title: How to Communicate with Empathy (free mini-class)
entryVideo.whyThisOne: A full class rather than a clip, so you can see whether a structured academic approach suits you before going further.

categories.why: Covers interpersonal basics in a numbered, teachable form that works well if you want to practise one element at a time.
categories.evidence: A recurring series on interpersonal communication skills built for classroom use rather than for engagement.

entryVideo.title: 5 Effective Interpersonal Communication Skills
entryVideo.whyThisOne: Five discrete skills you can work through separately, which suits deliberate practice better than a single narrative video.

categories.why: Applies a plain decision framework to workplace reasoning, aimed at people who have never been taught this formally.
categories.evidence: Dedicated videos on critical thinking and problem-solving frameworks, taught from his teaching practice rather than as commentary.

entryVideo.title: Improve Your Critical Thinking With This Framework
entryVideo.whyThisOne: A single framework explained end to end, which is enough to judge whether the academic register is useful to you.

name: Andrew Huang
shortDescription: A working multi-genre musician whose channel mixes real production technique with a great deal of entertainment and experiment.
longDescription: Andrew Huang describes himself as a partially deaf musician from Toronto working across many genres and instruments, and lists a plugin developed with Baby Audio, a sampler app, a book and an online production class. The channel matches that range and is not primarily a teaching channel: a hundred and thirty of the last two hundred uploads run two minutes or less and the median is one minute. What sits behind the short-form is a mixture of genuine technique videos, collaborations where several producers work the same brief, and studio experiments that are closer to entertainment than instruction. The value for a learner is exposure — hearing many approaches to the same problem from someone fluent in all of them — with the caveat that you will have to sift.
notFor: Anyone wanting a structured production curriculum. The signal-to-entertainment ratio is low and nothing here is sequenced.

categories.why: Shows many valid routes to the same musical result, which breaks the beginner assumption that there is one correct way to make a sound.
categories.evidence: A working musician and plugin developer whose catalogue includes sound-design tutorials alongside multi-producer collaborations on shared briefs.

entryVideo.title: How to make HUGE 808s!
entryVideo.whyThisOne: One of the plainly instructional videos on a channel that is often not, and the technique is reusable in any DAW.

caveats: Mostly short-form and often entertainment rather than teaching. Sells a production class, a book, an app and a plugin, all promoted on the channel.

name: Vinh Giang
shortDescription: An Australian communication coach who teaches vocal delivery, body language and conversational technique, mostly through very short clips with a smaller long-form catalogue behind them.
longDescription: Vinh Giang is a communication coach based in Australia who came to speaking through stage magic, and now runs paid workshops and masterclasses alongside the channel. His own account of his background is a decade of speaking work, large-audience appearances and executive coaching — practitioner experience rather than an academic credential. The content is drills and technique: vocal exercises, filler-word habits, posture, small talk openings, and how status is read from how you speak. Output is now overwhelmingly short-form, around forty of the last fifty uploads running a minute or less, though roughly thirty substantial videos of five to thirty minutes sit in the back catalogue and are where the actual teaching happens.
notFor: Anyone wanting claims tied to published research, or a structured curriculum rather than a feed of one-minute clips you have to assemble yourself.

categories.why: Drills the mechanics of speaking while people are watching you — pace, pauses, the voice itself, and what to do with the nerves rather than how to suppress them.
categories.evidence: Works as a professional speaking coach and has built the channel's long-form catalogue around delivery under attention, including frameworks on speaking habits and first impressions.

entryVideo.title: How to Speak When All Eyes Are On You...
entryVideo.whyThisOne: The longest and most structured thing on the channel about performing under attention, so you can judge the teaching style before committing to anything else.

categories.why: Treats presence as adjustable behaviour — warmth against authority, and the habits that quietly make people read you as lower status.
categories.evidence: A run of videos on first impressions, likeability versus respect, and status signals in speech, drawn from his workshop material.

entryVideo.title: How to Be Likeable AND Respected
entryVideo.whyThisOne: Covers the warmth-and-competence trade-off directly, which is the useful frame for anyone who comes across as one but not the other.

categories.why: Practical openings and recovery moves for one-to-one conversation, aimed squarely at people who find the start of them hard.
categories.evidence: Regular long-form material on small talk, question-asking and conversational repair, distinct from his stage-speaking content.

entryVideo.title: How to Master Any Conversation (Even If You’re an Introvert)
entryVideo.whyThisOne: Aimed at people who dislike small talk rather than people who already enjoy it, so it is the honest starting point for most viewers.

caveats: Sells communication workshops and masterclasses, which the channel funnels toward; the free material is usable on its own.

name: Barbell Medicine
shortDescription: Physicians who lift, spending much of their time dismantling the claims the rest of the fitness industry repeats.
longDescription: Barbell Medicine describes itself as the integration of medicine, lifestyle modification and strength training, and its distinguishing habit is going after specific popular claims rather than offering an alternative programme. Recent output includes named takedowns — the set-point myth in weight regulation, the cortisol myth in menopause — alongside plain-language explanations of large training studies and of what detraining actually costs you. A hundred of the last two hundred uploads are shorts and thirty-seven run past twenty minutes, where the argument lives. The register is clinical and unexcited, which is the point: this is the corrective to a field where confident claims travel faster than the evidence behind them.
notFor: Anyone wanting a programme handed over, or motivation. They will more often tell you a question is unsettled than give you a number.

categories.why: Reads the actual training literature and reports what it supports, including when the answer is less certain than the industry implies.
categories.evidence: Physicians publishing explanations of large resistance-training studies and of detraining effects, alongside named myth corrections in adjacent health topics.

entryVideo.title: The Biggest Resistance-Training Study in 17 Years, Explained
entryVideo.whyThisOne: One major study explained properly, which shows how they handle evidence better than any summary of their views could.

categories.why: Corrects the confident numbers that circulate about muscle gain and loss, which is the most common source of wasted training decisions.
categories.evidence: Videos on detraining and muscle memory, and on what actually determines bodyweight, framed explicitly against widely repeated myths.

entryVideo.title: How Fast Do You Lose Muscle? Detraining and Muscle Memory
entryVideo.whyThisOne: Answers a question almost everyone has been given a wrong confident answer to, and shows the working.

caveats: Sells coaching, programming and seminars. Small channel, dry delivery, and heavily short-form — the long-form material takes finding.

name: Benjamin Keep
shortDescription: A cognitive scientist who spends much of his time explaining why popular learning advice — including the advice everyone repeats — does not survive the research.
longDescription: Benjamin Keep describes himself as a cognitive scientist specialising in learning and instruction, and the channel's distinguishing feature is how often it argues against things. Deliberate practice, memory-athlete techniques, the study habits circulating on this very corner of YouTube — each gets a video examining what the evidence actually supports and where the popular version overreaches. He is not a contrarian: the videos are careful, specific about which claim is failing, and willing to say when the popular version is broadly right. The format is consistent and short by learning-channel standards, with a hundred and seven of a hundred and fifteen videos running three to nineteen minutes and a median of eight. Nothing new since April 2026.
notFor: Anyone wanting a study system handed to them. He is more likely to complicate the technique you arrived with than to replace it.

categories.why: Takes apart the popularised version of deliberate practice specifically, and says which parts the research supports and which were added in translation.
categories.evidence: Multiple videos examining deliberate practice as a construct, including one on what people get wrong about it and one questioning it outright, from a cognitive scientist specialising in learning.

entryVideo.title: What People Get Wrong About Deliberate Practice
entryVideo.whyThisOne: Nine minutes that will change how you read every other practice-related recommendation on this site.

categories.why: The direct counterweight to memory-sport instruction — argues that copying competitors is the wrong move for most people, and explains what to do instead.
categories.evidence: A video arguing specifically against copying memory athletes, alongside research-led pieces on what makes material memorable in the first place.

entryVideo.title: Two Reasons NOT to Copy Memory Athletes
entryVideo.whyThisOne: Watch it next to Nelson Dellis and you have the argument from both sides, which is the honest way to approach this category.

categories.why: Treats reading difficulty as a solvable technical problem rather than a stamina failure, which is more useful than any advice about reading more.
categories.evidence: Dedicated videos on reading with precision and on what to do when reading gets hard, grounded in his instructional-science background.

entryVideo.title: A short guide to reading with extreme precision
entryVideo.whyThisOne: A concrete method for hard text, which is the situation where general reading advice stops helping.

caveats: Dormant since April 2026. The register is academic and he rarely tells you what to do — the value is in dismantling bad advice, not replacing it.

name: Better Ideas (Joey Schweitzer)
shortDescription: Self-improvement essays that keep circling back to why the previous advice failed, including his own.
longDescription: Joey Schweitzer's channel is small and consistent — a hundred and thirty videos, a hundred and nineteen of them between three and nineteen minutes, median ten — and it occupies an unusual position in the genre. The subject matter is standard enough on paper: habits, procrastination, routines, the mechanics of changing behaviour. What distinguishes it is a persistent reflexivity, including a video reacting to the worst advice he has previously given on his own channel. That willingness to revisit is rare in a field where old videos are quietly left up. The register is casual and essayistic rather than instructional, so you get an argument to think with rather than a protocol.
notFor: Anyone wanting a system or a checklist. This is one person reasoning out loud about behaviour change, and it is deliberately unsystematic.

categories.why: Focuses on the single mistake that makes most habit attempts collapse, rather than on stacking more habits onto a life that is already failing to hold them.
categories.evidence: A run of videos on habit construction and its failure modes, including a dedicated piece on the biggest habit-building mistake and one on habits that quietly degrade a life.

entryVideo.title: The biggest habit building mistake
entryVideo.whyThisOne: Diagnoses the failure before offering a method, which is the right order and the one most habit content skips.

categories.why: Willing to say that the answer people want to hear is not the answer, which is a useful counterweight to trick-based procrastination advice.
categories.evidence: Multiple videos on procrastination, including one explicitly framed as the cure viewers do not want to hear and one revisiting his own earlier bad advice.

entryVideo.title: The procrastination cure you don't want to hear
entryVideo.whyThisOne: Short, unflattering, and a fair test of whether you want this channel's register at all.

caveats: Entirely one person's experience with no research behind it, and the essay format means you extract the actionable part yourself.

name: Buzzsprout
shortDescription: A podcast-hosting company's channel: practical launch-and-growth guidance plus long interviews with people who make podcasts well.
longDescription: Buzzsprout hosts podcasts, and the channel exists to help its customers make them, which shapes everything about it. The output is mostly short — a hundred and forty-five of the last two hundred uploads run two minutes or less, with a median of one — and the mid-length material skews practical and occasionally dated, covering distribution, equipment, promotion and episode planning. The strongest content is the long-form interviews, in which a working podcaster walks through how their show is actually made; these run past an hour and are craft rather than logistics. This is the only substantial podcasting channel in the dataset so far, and it is a company channel, so read it as competent vendor education rather than as independent teaching.
notFor: Anyone wanting audio-production depth or independent tool comparisons; the host platform's own product is never going to lose a comparison here.

categories.why: Covers the whole unglamorous pipeline from recording to distribution, and the interviews show how a well-made show is actually assembled.
categories.evidence: A podcast host's education channel combining launch, equipment and promotion guidance with hour-plus interviews taking apart the production process of established shows.

entryVideo.title: How Jack Rhysider Creates Darknet Diaries
entryVideo.whyThisOne: A full walkthrough of how one genuinely well-made show gets built, which is worth more than any amount of general launch advice.

caveats: Vendor education for a hosting platform — treat any tool or platform recommendation accordingly. Much of the mid-length catalogue dates from 2022–23 and shows it.

name: ByteByteGo
shortDescription: Animated system-design explainers from the authors of the System Design Interview books — clear, consistent, and shaped by the interview format.
longDescription: ByteByteGo is run by Alex Xu and Sahn Lam, the authors of the System Design Interview book series, and the channel is the video expression of that work. The format is tight and consistent: a hundred and thirty-nine of its hundred and sixty-nine videos run three to nineteen minutes with a five-minute median, each taking one component or one design problem and working through it with animated diagrams. Coverage spans the standard vocabulary — caching, rate limiting, message queues, chat and feed architectures. Its strength and its limit are the same thing: the material is organised around what gets asked in interviews, which is a real and useful subset of system design rather than the whole discipline.
notFor: Anyone designing a system rather than being asked about one. The framing is interview-shaped, and real trade-offs are compressed for time.

categories.why: Gives you the shared vocabulary — what a rate limiter is, why a queue is there — which is the prerequisite for any design conversation.
categories.evidence: An animated catalogue covering standard distributed-system components and design problems, from the authors of the System Design Interview book series.

entryVideo.title: Rate Limiter System Design: Token Bucket, Leaky Bucket, Scaling
entryVideo.whyThisOne: One component, several named algorithms, and the trade-off between them — the clearest small example of the channel's method.

caveats: Interview-oriented, so depth is sacrificed for coverage. Sells books and a newsletter, and nearly every video routes to them.

name: Cal Newport
shortDescription: The academic who named deep work, in very long podcast form — arguments about attention and work culture rather than tactics.
longDescription: Cal Newport is a computer science professor at Georgetown and the author of Deep Work, Digital Minimalism and A World Without Email, which is unusual grounding for this genre: the ideas most productivity channels repeat second-hand originate here. The channel is his podcast, and the format is demanding — a hundred and seventy-four of the last two hundred uploads run past twenty minutes, with a median of sixty-nine and many past an hour. Nothing is short. The content is argument and listener questions rather than instruction: why attention is structured the way it is, why email became the organising medium of knowledge work, what a deliberately constructed life looks like. You are being reasoned with at length, not given a checklist.
notFor: Anyone with less than an hour, or who wants tactics. The ideas are strong; the delivery is a professor talking, and it does not compress.

categories.why: This is the primary source for the concept everything else in the category is quoting, argued by the person who defined it — including how to put the work in the hours you can actually do it.
categories.evidence: A Georgetown computer science professor and author of Deep Work, publishing extended treatments of concentration and scheduling on his own podcast.

entryVideo.title: Rules For Deep Work — Updated for 2026 | Cal Newport
entryVideo.whyThisOne: His own framework restated and revised years on, which is more useful than the original because he says what he got wrong.

categories.why: Frames technology use as a set of deliberate decisions about what earns access to your attention, rather than as abstinence.
categories.evidence: Author of Digital Minimalism, with sustained podcast material on attention, technology and constructing a deliberate life.

entryVideo.title: Cultivate A Deep Life: One Idea To Change How You Think About Life In 2025 | Cal Newport
entryVideo.whyThisOne: The philosophical case underneath the practical advice, which is what makes any of the tactics stick.

categories.why: Treats email as a structural problem in how knowledge work is organised, not as a personal failure to process messages faster.
categories.evidence: Author of A World Without Email, with multiple full episodes on inbox overload and process-centric alternatives to ad-hoc messaging.

entryVideo.title: The Real Reason You Hate Your Inbox | Deep Questions with Cal Newport
entryVideo.whyThisOne: Nine minutes — rare on this channel — stating the structural diagnosis before the long-form arguments.

addedLater.trigger: inbox-and-email-systems was empty after the batch-08 first pass and I checked creators already in the batch.
addedLater.whyNotAtFirstPass: Honest answer: the trigger was gap-filling rather than new evidence, and this one is hard to excuse — he wrote A World Without Email, so the mapping should have been obvious immediately. It was missed because I anchored on the two other books of his I had already used to justify the deep-work and digital-minimalism mappings, and stopped looking.

caveats: Extremely long episodes with a lot of listener questions between the ideas. Promotes his books persistently, and his positions on technology are contested.

name: CareerVidz (Richard McMunn)
shortDescription: Two decades of interview coaching turned into a very large library of questions, model answers and role-specific preparation.
longDescription: Richard McMunn founded the channel in 2011 and its stated basis is two decades of his own careers and interview expertise. The catalogue is nearly three thousand videos and is organised the way a candidate actually searches: by question, by role, by employer type. Sixteen of fifty recent uploads run three to nineteen minutes and fourteen run past twenty, with a nine-minute median, so items are substantial enough to work through. The model-answer format is the strength and the weakness together — it gives you a shape to adapt when you have never seen one, and it will make you sound like everyone else if you recite it. The role-specific material goes unusually deep into particular jobs rather than staying generic.
notFor: Anyone wanting to develop their own answers from first principles, or working in a field where scripted responses are penalised.

categories.why: Gives you the shape of a competent answer to questions you will actually be asked, which is what most people lack the first few times.
categories.evidence: A nearly three-thousand-video interview library founded on two decades of stated careers and interview coaching, organised by question and by role.

entryVideo.title: 11 INTERVIEW QUESTIONS YOU MUST PREPARE FOR! (Best Answers Included!)
entryVideo.whyThisOne: The eleven questions that recur across almost every interview, with worked answers to adapt rather than recite.

caveats: Sells guides and courses throughout. Model answers are widely watched, so reciting them verbatim is a real risk — adapt rather than memorise.

name: Carl Pullein
shortDescription: A time-management author with a named system, weekly output, and an unusual insistence that your calendar tells the truth and your to-do list does not.
longDescription: Carl Pullein's channel description sets out his credentials plainly: author of Your Time Your Way, creator of the Time Sector System and the Collect–Organise–Do method, and founder of his own training practice. He has published weekly for years, accumulating over thirteen hundred videos. The recurring argument is a useful corrective to task-management culture — that a to-do list conceals how much time you actually have, that most people are overcommitted without having noticed, and that the fix is a decision about what not to do rather than a better app. Output has gone short, with a hundred and seven of the last two hundred uploads under two minutes and a median of two, but eighty-eight remain in the mid-length band where the reasoning is.
notFor: Anyone looking for the newest app. He teaches one system and is fairly insistent about it, and the presentation is plain to the point of dry.

categories.why: Organises commitments by when they must be done rather than by project or context, and treats the recurring review as the thing that keeps the system trustworthy.
categories.evidence: Author of a published time-management book and creator of two named systems, taught across a thirteen-hundred-video catalogue including full setups in specific task managers.

entryVideo.title: The Ultimate Todoist Setup: Filters, Labels, and Time Sectors
entryVideo.whyThisOne: The system implemented concretely in a real tool, so you can judge whether it survives contact with your actual work.

categories.why: Argues that the shortage is time rather than organisation, so the only real move is deciding what not to do — and he is specific about how.
categories.evidence: Repeated videos on overcommitment and on the gap between a to-do list and available time, consistent with the time-sector approach he authored.

entryVideo.title: Your To-Do List Is Hiding the Truth About Your Time
entryVideo.whyThisOne: Twelve minutes on the specific way a task list flatters you, which is the diagnosis before any prioritisation method makes sense.

categories.why: Gives a concrete repeatable routine for emptying an inbox, which pairs usefully with the structural critique rather than replacing it.
categories.evidence: Dedicated videos on clearing an inbox to zero as a timed routine, within his published time-management system.

entryVideo.title: How to Clear Your Entire Inbox in Under 6 Minutes
entryVideo.whyThisOne: A mechanical routine you can run today, as the practical counterpart to Cal Newport's argument that the problem is structural.

addedLater.trigger: inbox-and-email-systems needed a second creator, to pair a practical routine against Cal Newport's structural critique.
addedLater.whyNotAtFirstPass: Gap-filling again. His inbox-zero routine was already in the evidence gathered for his record; it went unmapped because I built the record around his time-sector system and stopped at three categories.

caveats: Sells courses and coaching around his own named systems, and the channel exists partly to do that. Heavily short-form now.

name: Chandoo
shortDescription: Long-running Excel and analytics teaching aimed at making you effective at work, including comparisons that admit when the spreadsheet is the wrong tool.
longDescription: Chandoo has taught Excel and analytics for well over a decade, and the channel's stated purpose is straightforwardly practical: making you good at your job with Excel, Power BI, SQL and Python. Six hundred videos, and the format sits in a useful middle range — dashboard construction, pivot tables taught in a single sitting, and specific function deep dives. What distinguishes it from the tips genre is a willingness to compare tools against each other and concede the limits of spreadsheets, including head-to-head comparisons of Power Query against Python on the same task. That honesty is rare in a field where the teacher's whole business depends on the tool.
notFor: Anyone wanting a structured beginner course; this is a large archive organised by topic, and browsing it without a specific problem is unrewarding.

categories.why: Teaches spreadsheets as one tool among several and shows where they stop being the right one, which most Excel channels never concede.
categories.evidence: A decade-plus Excel and analytics catalogue including direct comparisons of spreadsheet tooling against Python on the same data-cleaning task.

entryVideo.title: Excel Pivot Tables in 10mins (free workbook)
entryVideo.whyThisOne: The single highest-leverage Excel feature, taught in one sitting with a workbook to practise on.

caveats: Sells courses and a membership. Note the name is heavily collided on YouTube — this is `@chandoo_`; `@chandootalks` is a lifestyle vlogger with more uploads.

name: Charisma on Command
shortDescription: Breaks down charisma and social confidence by analysing clips of well-known people frame by frame, then naming the specific behaviour that produced the effect.
longDescription: Charisma on Command has been publishing since the mid-2010s and has settled into a consistent format: take a piece of footage of someone widely read as charismatic or awkward, slow it down, and isolate the behaviour doing the work. Unusually for a channel this size, the output is genuinely long-form — around a hundred and ninety of the last two hundred uploads run between three and nineteen minutes, with a median of eleven. The analysis is behavioural rather than research-led: it describes what someone did and why it landed, without claiming an experimental basis. It suits people who learn better from worked examples than from principles, and who want something more concrete than advice to be confident.
notFor: Anyone who wants cited evidence rather than close reading of clips, or who finds celebrity-analysis framing a distraction from practising the skill itself.

categories.why: The channel's core subject, treated as a set of observable behaviours you can copy rather than a personality you either have or lack.
categories.evidence: Ten years of long-form videos dissecting how specific people generate warmth, authority and attention, which is the whole editorial premise of the channel.

entryVideo.title: If You Only Watch One Charisma Video, Make It This
entryVideo.whyThisOne: Their own attempt at a single summary of the method, so it is the fastest way to decide whether the analytical approach works for you.

categories.why: Unusually concrete on the opening seconds of a conversation, where most advice stays abstract about being interested rather than interesting.
categories.evidence: Repeated dedicated long-form videos on small talk, group entry and conversational exits, separate from the charisma analysis.

entryVideo.title: Give Me 7 Minutes and I’ll Make You Dangerously Good at Small Talk
entryVideo.whyThisOne: Covers openings, sustaining and exits in one pass, so you get the whole shape of a conversation rather than a single trick.

categories.why: Separates looking confident from being confident, and argues the performance is the weaker of the two — a useful corrective in this genre.
categories.evidence: Several long-form videos specifically about performed versus actual confidence, including material arguing against the channel's own earlier framing.

entryVideo.title: Identity Protection Is Killing Your Confidence, Do This Instead
entryVideo.whyThisOne: The clearest statement of their position that confidence signalling backfires, which is worth hearing before you copy any technique.

caveats: Sells a paid confidence course, and a slice of the catalogue is framed around masculinity and dating, which sits oddly beside the general-audience material.

name: Chewjitsu (Nick Albin)
shortDescription: Brazilian jiu-jitsu technique and, unusually, the training culture around it — including how to survive being a beginner.
longDescription: Chewjitsu covers grappling technique and the lifestyle around training, and its distinguishing feature is how much attention goes to the non-technical problems: what to do about training partners who go too hard, the ego traps coaches fall into, how to keep training as you get older. A hundred and fifty-six of the last two hundred uploads run three to nineteen minutes at a seven-minute median, so the format is a focused answer rather than a full seminar. Technical content is organised around what a beginner actually needs — escapes before submissions, positions before flashy sequences — which is the correct order and not the order most jiu-jitsu content follows.
notFor: Anyone wanting competition-level systems or a structured curriculum; this is a large archive of individual answers, not a syllabus.

categories.why: Teaches escapes and survival before submissions, and takes the social side of a gym seriously — both of which decide whether a beginner keeps training.
categories.evidence: A large grappling catalogue ordered around beginner needs, including escape sequences, guard strategy for older trainees, and material on training-partner and coaching culture.

entryVideo.title: The First 5 Mount Escapes You Need to Know in BJJ
entryVideo.whyThisOne: The single position beginners spend the most time stuck under, with the escapes in the order you will need them.

caveats: Sells instructional courses and a membership. Nothing here is evidence-based in any formal sense — it is one experienced coach's judgement.

name: Coffeezilla
shortDescription: Investigations into scams and self-styled gurus, showing the paper trail rather than asserting that something smells wrong.
longDescription: Coffeezilla's own channel description states the remit plainly: uncovering scams, fraudsters and fake gurus preying on people with deceptive advertising. The output is steady and mid-length — a hundred and fifty-one of the last two hundred uploads run three to nineteen minutes, with forty-two past twenty. The method is investigative rather than rhetorical: he buys into the thing, reads the filings, traces the wallets, and confronts the people involved on camera, often getting them to say something they later regret. Recent subjects skew toward crypto, celebrity promotions and gambling rather than the classic self-improvement guru, but the transferable part is the discipline of asking where the money actually goes when someone tells you they can teach you to be rich.
notFor: Anyone wanting a general method for evaluating claims; this is one investigator on one type of target, and the framing is prosecutorial by design.

categories.why: Gives you a single transferable question — where does the money actually come from — and shows it being applied to people who sound extremely convincing.
categories.evidence: A channel whose stated purpose is investigating fake gurus and deceptive advertising, with episodes tracing specific schemes through filings, wallets and on-camera confrontations.

entryVideo.title: Exposing Andrew Tate’s Crypto Grift
entryVideo.whyThisOne: Sixteen minutes on a figure whose whole business is selling self-improvement, which makes it the most directly relevant thing here for anyone using a site like this one.

caveats: The register is adversarial and the thumbnails are tabloid. Subjects are chosen partly for how well they perform, so absence from the channel is not evidence of anything.

name: Conor Neill
shortDescription: A business-school lecturer in Spain with a long back catalogue on speaking and persuasion, whose newer output has moved toward leadership.
longDescription: Conor Neill teaches at a business school in Spain and has been uploading since long before most communication channels existed, which gives the channel an unusual shape: four hundred and twenty-four videos, most of them short, and a clear split between eras. The older material is the reason to be here — a long run of short, plain videos on speaking mechanics, audience types, handling a hostile room, managing anxiety before you go on, and the difference between persuading and manipulating. The recent two hundred uploads have drifted toward leadership, goal-setting and executive coaching, with a median length of six minutes. Nothing is heavily produced; it is mostly one person talking to a camera about something he teaches.
notFor: Anyone wanting the current uploads to be about speaking — they mostly are not, and the speaking material takes some digging in the archive.

categories.why: Short, unglamorous videos on the specific mechanics — audience types, hostile rooms, how much to rehearse — from someone who teaches this to MBA students.
categories.evidence: A sustained run of speaking-specific videos in the back catalogue covering audience analysis, anxiety before speaking, hostile audiences and rehearsal, alongside his business-school teaching.

entryVideo.title: How to Handle Anxiety (especially when speaking in public)
entryVideo.whyThisOne: Eight minutes on the thing that actually stops most people speaking, and short enough to watch before you need it.

categories.why: Draws the line between persuading someone and manipulating them explicitly, which most persuasion content leaves comfortably blurred.
categories.evidence: A video dedicated to the persuasion-versus-manipulation distinction, plus longer sessions on pitching and on storytelling as persuasion.

entryVideo.title: Persuasion vs Manipulation  | Conor Neill | Leadership
entryVideo.whyThisOne: The ethical question first, before any technique — a useful order, and unusual for the genre.

caveats: Production is basic and the archive is poorly organised. Promotes his own courses and his executive-coaching work.

name: ContraPoints
shortDescription: A former philosophy academic making a handful of very long, heavily staged essays on how people come to believe and want things.
longDescription: ContraPoints describes herself simply as a YouTuber and ex-philosopher, and the channel is unusually small for its size: thirty-six videos in total, thirty-one of them over twenty minutes and a median of thirty-two, with several past ninety and one past two and a half hours. The essays are theatrical — costumes, sets, characters arguing with each other — which is a genuine method rather than decoration, because the recurring subject is how a position feels from the inside. Titles are single words: Envy, Shame, Cringe, Conspiracy, Justice, Canceling. The philosophical training shows in the structure; she will steelman a view at length before turning on it, which is exactly the discipline the reasoning categories are about and exactly what most debunking content skips.
notFor: Anyone who wants brevity or neutrality. These are long, stylised, and argued from an explicit left-wing and trans perspective that she does not pretend to set aside.

categories.why: Practises steelmanning as performance — inhabiting a belief convincingly before dismantling it — which is far harder and more instructive than refutation from outside.
categories.evidence: A small catalogue of very long philosophical essays, made by a former academic philosopher, that repeatedly construct the strongest version of a position before arguing against it.

entryVideo.title: Conspiracy | ContraPoints
entryVideo.whyThisOne: Directly about why conspiracy reasoning is appealing rather than why it is stupid — but it is two hours and forty minutes, so plan for that.

caveats: Extremely long videos and an explicit political position. Uploads are rare — a few per year — so this is a back catalogue to work through, not a feed.

name: Corey Schafer
shortDescription: Long, unhurried Python tutorials that explain the language properly rather than racing to a finished app — the closest thing here to a textbook on video.
longDescription: Corey Schafer's channel is built on a format almost nobody else sustains: a hundred and twenty-six of the last two hundred uploads run past twenty minutes, with a median of twenty-four, and several past an hour. The subject matter is Python taught in depth — iterators, classes, the standard library, the parts of the language people work around for years rather than learning. Alongside that sits a long multi-part FastAPI series that builds a full application end to end across sixteen episodes, which is where the backend material lives. The pace is deliberate and the presentation is plain: a screen, a voice, and an explanation that does not skip the part you were about to be confused by.
notFor: Anyone in a hurry or wanting current-framework coverage; uploads are infrequent, and depth is prioritised over keeping up with what is new.

categories.why: Teaches the language itself rather than a stack built on it, and gives each concept the running time to actually land.
categories.evidence: A long-running Python tutorial catalogue covering language fundamentals, classes and standard-library modules in dedicated episodes, with a twenty-four-minute median length.

entryVideo.title: Python Tutorial: Itertools Module - Iterator Functions for Efficient Looping
entryVideo.whyThisOne: A standard-library module most self-taught developers never open, taught in full — a fair sample of the depth on offer.

categories.why: Builds one real API across a long series instead of a toy, so authentication, migrations and deployment appear where they actually do in a project.
categories.evidence: A sixteen-part FastAPI series covering routing, authentication, PostgreSQL migrations, pagination and cloud file storage as sequential episodes.

entryVideo.title: Python FastAPI Tutorial (Part 15): PostgreSQL and Alembic - Database Migrations for Production
entryVideo.whyThisOne: Migrations are the part every tutorial skips and every real project needs — this is where the series proves it is not a toy.

caveats: Infrequent uploads and some older material references dated library versions. Almost no coverage of the current framework churn.

name: Database Star (Ben Brumm)
shortDescription: Practical SQL for people who already write it — performance rules, real query post-mortems, and the business calculations nobody teaches.
longDescription: Database Star is a small, focused channel about writing SQL well rather than about learning what SELECT does. Three hundred and forty-three videos, most in the short-to-mid range, and the recurring formats are useful ones: named rules for high-performance queries, worked post-mortems of a specific query that was quietly costing something, and calculations people actually need at work such as revenue and churn metrics expressed in SQL. That last category is rare — most SQL teaching stops at syntax and never shows what a real analytical question looks like written out. Production values are modest and the channel is small, which is not the same as being wrong.
notFor: Absolute beginners who have never written a query, and anyone needing database administration rather than SQL itself.

categories.why: Focuses on making queries fast and correct in production, with worked examples of real queries that were quietly wrong or expensive.
categories.evidence: A SQL-focused catalogue including named performance rules, post-mortems of specific costly queries, and analytical calculations written out in full.

entryVideo.title: The 7 Rules for Writing High-Performance SQL
entryVideo.whyThisOne: Seven checkable rules you can apply to a query you already have, which makes it immediately testable.

caveats: Small channel with basic production. Sells courses, and the coverage assumes a relational database rather than anything newer.

name: Andy Stapleton
shortDescription: Academic-career and research-workflow advice from a former academic, now heavily focused on AI tools — including their failure modes.
longDescription: Andy Stapleton's channel is about navigating academia: publishing, supervision, the parts of the process nobody explains to a new postgraduate. A hundred and forty-three of the last two hundred uploads run between three and nineteen minutes with a median of eleven, and the current centre of gravity is unmistakably AI tooling for research — comparisons of assistants, prompting technique for literature work, and, usefully, videos on where those tools produce something that looks like scholarship but is not. That last strand is what earns him a place here rather than disqualifying him: he is specific about how an AI-generated literature review fails. Anyone wanting timeless writing craft rather than current tooling will find the ratio frustrating.
notFor: Anyone outside academia, or looking for durable writing instruction; a large share of this is about tools that will look dated within a year.

categories.why: Deals with the research process as it is actually done now, including how to use the current tools without letting them do your thinking.
categories.evidence: A former academic publishing workflow guidance on searching, prompting and assessing sources for research, alongside supervision and publishing advice.

entryVideo.title: You SUCK at Prompting AI For Research (Do This instead)
entryVideo.whyThisOne: Concrete technique for a tool most researchers are now using badly, with the failure modes named rather than glossed.

categories.why: Its most useful contribution to writing is negative — showing what an automated literature review actually produces and why it will not pass.
categories.evidence: Videos examining AI-produced literature reviews and their specific deficiencies, within a catalogue on publishing and thesis work.

entryVideo.title: This Free AI Wrote My Entire Literature Review in Minutes (Why That's a Problem)
entryVideo.whyThisOne: Demonstrates the shortcut and then dismantles it, which is more persuasive than being told not to take it.

caveats: Heavily AI-tool focused and will date quickly. Sells coaching and courses, and the channel found here is @drandystapleton — @AndyStapleton is a near-empty 2-video channel.

name: Dreaming Spanish
languageNote: The uploads are in Spanish, not English — deliberately. This is a comprehensible-input channel, where hearing the target language you can almost follow IS the teaching method, so an English version of these videos would not be the same resource. Included under the named exemption in project rule 5. No prior Spanish is assumed: the beginner videos are built to be understood from context, gesture and drawing alone.
shortDescription: Spanish taught entirely in Spanish, pitched so that a total beginner can follow from context — the comprehensible-input method done at scale.
longDescription: Dreaming Spanish teaches by immersion: you watch content at a level you can just about understand and work upward, which its own description frames as learning the way you learned your first language. In practice that means a speaker on camera telling a simple story, drawing on a whiteboard, gesturing, and staying inside a controlled vocabulary — no English, no grammar tables, no translation. The catalogue is graded by difficulty from superbeginner upward, and there is a lot of it: eight hundred videos, with a hundred and one of the last two hundred running three to nineteen minutes and eighty past twenty, at a fifteen-minute median. The method asks for patience and volume rather than study, and it is genuinely uncomfortable at the start, which is the part most learners are not warned about.
notFor: Anyone who wants grammar explained, translations given, or fast visible progress; the first weeks feel like watching something you do not understand, because that is what you are doing.

categories.why: The largest well-graded body of comprehensible input in one place, which turns the immersion method from a theory you read about into something you can actually do tonight.
categories.evidence: Eight hundred uploads graded by difficulty from superbeginner upward, delivered entirely in the target language using controlled vocabulary, drawing and gesture, per the channel's own stated method.

entryVideo.title: Spanish Story for Beginners | "The Angry Artist" | Level: Easy
entryVideo.whyThisOne: Eight minutes at the easiest level — the honest test of whether you can follow a language you do not yet speak, which is the whole premise.

caveats: Committed to one method and dismissive of alternatives; sells an app and a subscription. Spanish only — the approach generalises, this channel does not.

name: Dr. Mary Claire Haver
shortDescription: A board-certified OB-GYN on menopause and perimenopause, filling a gap she says clinical practice was leaving open.
longDescription: Dr. Mary Claire Haver describes herself as a board-certified OB-GYN with over twenty years in clinical practice, and states the channel's reason for existing directly: too many women were not getting clear answers elsewhere. The subject is menopause and perimenopause specifically — symptoms, treatment options, and the interactions people are rarely told about, such as how menopause intersects with ADHD. Format is barbelled: thirty-nine of fifty recent uploads are clips of under two minutes, while ten run past twenty and are substantial interviews with other specialists. That structure means the depth is real but concentrated. This is one clinician's synthesis rather than a survey of the literature, and it is squarely aimed at one population.
notFor: Anyone outside the menopause and perimenopause question, and anyone wanting the underlying research rather than a specialist's reading of it.

categories.why: Covers a hormonal transition most people get no usable information about, from a clinician who specialises in it rather than mentions it.
categories.evidence: A board-certified OB-GYN of twenty-plus years' practice publishing menopause and perimenopause education, including long specialist interviews on symptoms and treatment.

entryVideo.title: Top Menopause & Perimenopause Questions Answered
entryVideo.whyThisOne: Twenty minutes covering the questions people actually arrive with, which is the right orientation before the specialist interviews.

caveats: Sells books and a supplement-adjacent product line, so weigh product mentions accordingly. Almost entirely short-form, and narrow by design.

name: Dr. Tracey Marks
shortDescription: A board-certified psychiatrist translating neuroscience into short, plain explanations — heavily short-form, so treat it as reference rather than curriculum.
longDescription: Dr. Tracey Marks describes herself as a board-certified psychiatrist with more than twenty years of experience, translating neuroscience and psychiatry into practical tools for attention, emotional regulation and recovery under pressure. The channel is very large and very short: a hundred and seventy-four of the last two hundred uploads run two minutes or less, twenty-six sit in the three-to-nineteen band, and none in that window exceed twenty minutes. That format suits the material, which is mostly explanatory — what a symptom is, whether a difficulty is one thing or another, how a mechanism works — rather than instructional. Its best use is looking something up, not working through anything.
notFor: Anyone wanting depth or a course. Nothing here runs long, and the format rewards specific questions rather than sustained study.

categories.why: Explains what is mechanically happening rather than what to do about it, which is what you want when you are trying to work out whether something is worth seeing someone about.
categories.evidence: A psychiatrist of twenty-plus years publishing explanatory videos distinguishing stress, attention problems and clinical presentations from one another.

entryVideo.title: Why You Can't Focus: Is It ADHD or Just Stress?
entryVideo.whyThisOne: A distinction people get wrong constantly, drawn by someone qualified to draw it.

caveats: Almost entirely short-form, so nothing here is a substitute for depth. Explanatory rather than practical — it names the problem, it does not treat it.

name: Duarte, Inc.
shortDescription: The channel of a presentation consultancy that has been building corporate talks since 1988, aimed squarely at people who present to executives.
longDescription: Duarte is a presentation and communication firm whose own description dates it to 1988 and positions it around work for large brands. The channel reflects that clientele: the material is about getting stakeholder buy-in, winning budget approval, presenting change to a team, and developing the presence that makes senior people listen. It is not about giving a wedding speech. Of two hundred recent uploads, about a hundred are a minute or less and eighty-one run three to nineteen minutes, which is where the teaching sits — short, structured, formula-shaped videos, often built by reverse-engineering a well-known talk. The commercial motive is unhidden; this is a consultancy demonstrating competence.
notFor: Anyone outside a corporate setting. Almost every example assumes you have stakeholders, a budget request, or an executive audience.

categories.why: Reverse-engineers talks that demonstrably worked, and gives you the structure rather than an exhortation to be more confident.
categories.evidence: A consultancy building presentations for large organisations since 1988, whose channel breaks down the structure of specific well-known talks and executive presentations.

entryVideo.title: The Presentation Formula Behind Daniel Pink's 32M+ View TED Talk
entryVideo.whyThisOne: Takes one talk you can go and watch and shows the skeleton under it, which is the fastest way to start seeing structure in any talk.

categories.why: Applies story shape to business communication specifically — the case for a change, told so people move rather than nod.
categories.evidence: Repeated storytelling-for-business videos, including a run on communicating change through narrative rather than through slides of data.

entryVideo.title: Give me 7 minutes, and I'll improve your storytelling skills by 3x
entryVideo.whyThisOne: Eight minutes, one framework, and the claim is testable on your next update email.

categories.why: Treats presence as a set of nameable habits in a meeting rather than as a personality you either have or lack.
categories.evidence: A dedicated video on executive presence as four specific habits, consistent with the firm's coaching work with senior leaders.

entryVideo.title: How to Develop Executive Presence (4 Habits That Win a Room Fast)
entryVideo.whyThisOne: Names four things you can actually do differently on Monday, rather than describing what presence feels like.

caveats: This is marketing for a consultancy, and it shows in the framing. Note also that `@duarte` and `@duarteinc` are unrelated channels — this is the real one.

name: Dylan Johnson
shortDescription: Endurance training explained from the research by a racing cyclist and coach, including what he has changed his mind about.
longDescription: Dylan Johnson races and coaches, and the channel's method is consistent: take a training question, go to the exercise-physiology literature, and report what it supports. A hundred and fifty-seven of the last two hundred uploads run three to nineteen minutes with a thirteen-minute median, so the format is a focused argument rather than a vlog. Subjects include the training distribution debates, what the Norwegian endurance programme actually does differently, and whether hard training carries a long-term health cost. He also publishes reviews of his own previous training decisions and what went wrong, which is a useful antidote to a genre that mostly reports successes.
notFor: Anyone wanting bike handling, mechanics or gear reviews as the main event; this is training physiology, and it assumes you already ride.

categories.why: Answers training questions from the physiology literature rather than from what fast riders happen to do, and says when the evidence is thin.
categories.evidence: A racing cyclist and coach publishing research-led analyses of training distribution, national training methods and long-term training effects.

entryVideo.title: Why Does Norway Have So Many of the World's Best Endurance Athletes? The Norwegian Training Method
entryVideo.whyThisOne: A concrete case where the method is unusual and well documented, which makes the reasoning easy to follow and to test.

caveats: Sells coaching and training plans. The research framing can imply more certainty than endurance science actually offers, and gear content is creeping in.

name: E3 Rehab
shortDescription: Physical therapists publishing structured rehabilitation protocols and correcting the myths that keep people afraid to load an injury.
longDescription: E3 Rehab is run by Doctors of Physical Therapy whose stated approach is evidence-based education about rehabilitation, pain and injury risk. The long-form material is genuinely protocol-shaped rather than tip-shaped: full rehabilitation sequences for a region, criteria for returning to sport after specific injuries, and myth correction on conditions people are routinely frightened about. That last part matters, because fear of movement after an injury does more lasting damage than most of the injuries. A hundred and twenty-two of the last two hundred uploads are shorts and thirty-one run past twenty minutes. Nothing here replaces assessment by someone who can see you.
notFor: Anyone with an undiagnosed or acute injury. This is education about categories of problem, not advice about yours, and they say so.

categories.why: Gives return-to-activity criteria rather than a timeline, which is what actually determines whether you re-injure yourself.
categories.evidence: Doctors of Physical Therapy publishing full rehabilitation protocols and named criteria for returning to sport after specific injuries.

entryVideo.title: How To Return Back To Sport After An Injury (ACL, Meniscus, MCL, Ankle Sprain)
entryVideo.whyThisOne: The decision everyone gets wrong by guessing, handled with criteria instead of a number of weeks.

categories.why: Treats back pain with graded loading and education rather than protection, and dismantles the imaging-and-fragility story most people arrive with.
categories.evidence: A dedicated long-form lower-back rehabilitation video covering exercises, education, myths and prevention, from practising physical therapists.

entryVideo.title: Lower Back Pain Rehab (Exercises | Education | Myths | Prevention)
entryVideo.whyThisOne: The whole picture in one place — what to do, what to stop believing, and why loading is the treatment rather than the risk.

caveats: Sells programmes and consultations. Heavily short-form, and general education can never substitute for an assessment of your specific injury.

name: Effortless Swimming (Brenton Ford)
shortDescription: Freestyle technique analysed on video with real swimmers, from a coaching operation that has worked with thousands of them.
longDescription: The channel's stated basis is what they have learned coaching hundreds of athletes online and thousands more at clinics, and that shows in the format: technique explained against footage of actual swimmers, including the errors, rather than a demonstration by someone already excellent. The focus is freestyle mechanics — catch, arm recovery, body position, breathing — which is the stroke almost everyone needs and the one where small changes produce large efficiency gains. A hundred and sixty-four of the last two hundred uploads are under two minutes with a median of one, so the substantive coaching is a small share of the feed and includes long technical conversations with specialist coaches.
notFor: Anyone wanting a beginner's learn-to-swim course, or coverage of strokes other than freestyle in any depth.

categories.why: Analyses real swimmers on video rather than demonstrating a perfect stroke, so you can see the errors you are likely making.
categories.evidence: A coaching operation publishing freestyle mechanics breakdowns from clinic and online-coaching work with large numbers of swimmers, including technical sessions with specialist coaches.

entryVideo.title: How To Swim Freestyle With (Almost) Zero Effort
entryVideo.whyThisOne: The efficiency argument stated whole, which is the frame the rest of the technique work only makes sense inside.

caveats: Sells clinics, camps and online coaching, which most videos route toward. Now heavily short-form, and freestyle-dominated.

name: Exam Study Expert (William Wadsworth)
shortDescription: Exam technique built on learning science rather than study aesthetics — the rare channel here that treats sitting an exam as its own distinct skill.
longDescription: The channel's stated basis is the science of learning and memory applied to exams specifically: retrieval practice, spacing, and the psychology of performing on the day rather than merely knowing the material. That distinction is what makes it worth including — most study content teaches learning and assumes the exam takes care of itself. Eighty-five of the last two hundred uploads run past twenty minutes, largely podcast episodes including interviews with people whose work is high-pressure performance, and twenty-eight sit in the mid-length band. It is a small channel with a modest production budget, and the podcast format means a fair amount of conversation around each idea rather than a tight lesson.
notFor: Anyone not sitting exams. The material is genuinely exam-specific, and outside that context most of it does not transfer.

categories.why: Treats performing under exam conditions as a separate skill from knowing the material, which is the gap that catches out people who revised properly and still underperformed.
categories.evidence: A catalogue explicitly grounded in learning and memory research applied to exam technique, including dedicated material on exam pressure and psychological preparation.

entryVideo.title: 5 Mindset Shifts That Make Exams Less Stressful (A Psychologist Explains)
entryVideo.whyThisOne: Ten minutes on the performance half of the problem, which is the part revision timetables never address.

caveats: Sells coaching and courses. Small channel, podcast-heavy, so ideas arrive wrapped in a lot of conversation.

name: Film Riot
shortDescription: A long-running, deliberately energetic filmmaking how-to show, strongest on practical effects and on getting a scene shot at all.
longDescription: Film Riot has been running for well over a decade and has the archive to show for it — nearly thirteen hundred videos, with a hundred and eighty of the last two hundred sitting between three and nineteen minutes and a median of eleven. The channel's own description promises a how-to trip through filmmaking, and the emphasis has always been on doing rather than analysing: how to shoot a scene from camera settings through to coverage, how a zero-gravity effect was achieved, how classic films pulled off effects before digital tools existed. The tone is high-energy and comedic, which is either the appeal or the obstacle depending on you. Because the catalogue spans so many years, older episodes reference workflows and hardware that no longer exist.
notFor: Anyone who finds sketch-comedy framing distracting, or who wants film theory; this is a practical show about making things on small budgets.

categories.why: Covers the unglamorous mechanics of getting a scene in the can — settings, coverage, order of shots — which is where most first films actually fall apart.
categories.evidence: A thirteen-hundred-video how-to archive centred on production technique, including a numbered series on shooting a scene and long-running practical-effects breakdowns.

entryVideo.title: How to Film a Scene 101: Camera Settings to Coverage
entryVideo.whyThisOne: End-to-end on one scene rather than one isolated skill, which is the shape of the problem when you actually turn up to shoot.

caveats: The archive spans many years, so older episodes reference dead software and hardware. The comedic style is heavy and not to everyone's taste.

name: FitnessFAQs (Daniel Vadnal)
shortDescription: Calisthenics taught by a physiotherapist, with an unusual willingness to say a popular skill is a bad idea for most people.
longDescription: The channel's own description is four words of substance — hybrid calisthenics with a physiotherapist — and that combination is the reason to watch. Bodyweight training online is dominated by skill demonstrations; here the framing is progression and joint safety, including videos arguing that a widely chased skill like the one-arm pull-up carries risk that most people training toward it have not considered. Coverage runs through pull-up variations, alternatives when a movement is not available, and the shoulder work that makes the rest possible. Output has gone heavily short — a hundred and sixty-four of the last two hundred uploads are under two minutes — so the teaching sits in a minority of the feed.
notFor: Anyone wanting barbell strength work, or wanting to be told that any skill is achievable if you just train hard enough.

categories.why: Treats bodyweight skills as a progression with a joint cost, rather than as feats to attempt — which is the difference between training for years and getting injured in months.
categories.evidence: A physiotherapist publishing calisthenics progressions, movement alternatives and explicit cautions about the risks of commonly chased skills.

entryVideo.title: The Problem With One Arm Pull-Ups Is Dangerous
entryVideo.whyThisOne: Argues against the goal most calisthenics content sells you, from someone qualified to assess the risk.

caveats: Overwhelmingly short-form now. Sells programmes, and the physiotherapy framing is used commercially as well as clinically.

name: Folding Ideas (Dan Olson)
shortDescription: Long documentary essays that reconstruct how a false belief or a financial scheme was actually built, rather than just mocking the people inside it.
longDescription: Dan Olson describes himself as an Alberta-based documentarian making videos about stories and how they shape the world. The catalogue is a hundred and eighty-five videos with a median of eleven minutes, but the ones that matter here are the long investigations: forty-nine run past twenty minutes and several past seventy. The method is consistent and it is the reason to watch. He goes to the primary material — attends the flat-earth conference, buys the online course, reads the whitepaper, follows the money — and then reconstructs the internal logic of the thing before evaluating it. That order is the lesson. The subjects range from flat earth and creationist fossil claims to NFTs, get-rich-quick publishing schemes and video games, so a good deal of the channel is film and media criticism with no bearing on reasoning at all.
notFor: Anyone in a hurry, or who wants a set of rules for spotting nonsense; the videos are long, discursive, and the argument is the whole thing.

categories.why: Models the harder half of scepticism — taking a belief seriously enough to understand why it is convincing before explaining why it is wrong.
categories.evidence: Long primary-source investigations including a feature-length film on flat-earth belief made by attending the conference, a piece on fabricated fossil evidence, and an examination of an online course scheme.

entryVideo.title: In Search Of A Flat Earth
entryVideo.whyThisOne: Starts as a patient explanation of a fringe belief and turns into something much larger about how conspiracy thinking recruits — the turn is the point, so watch it whole.

caveats: Much of the catalogue is film and games criticism unrelated to reasoning. The long videos are genuinely long — treat one as an evening.

name: Gareth David Studio
shortDescription: A working creative director teaching graphic design as a commercial discipline with constraints, not as self-expression.
longDescription: Gareth David describes himself as a creative director with over fifteen years in the industry, making design content alongside the job. The channel's most useful trait is its insistence on framing: one of its recurring arguments is that graphic design is strategy rather than art, and the material follows from that — what the successful pieces have in common, how the different design jobs actually differ from each other, how to judge your own work against a brief instead of against taste.
